analysis.one_liner: Lets lawfully present immigrants, including DACA recipients, enroll in Medicaid, CHIP, and subsidized health plans.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would remove immigration-status barriers to health coverage. Lawfully present immigrants who meet income rules would become eligible for Medicaid and the Children's Health Insurance Program without waiting periods, and people with federal permission to be here, such as DACA recipients, would count as lawfully present for ACA marketplaces. It would also let them qualify for premium subsidies, reduced copays, and premium tax credits, and would remove the five-year residence wait and the ACA's exclusion of undocumented immigrants from marketplace plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Lawfully present immigrant families, including green-card holders in their first five years and DACA recipients, who currently face waiting periods or outright exclusion from Medicaid, CHIP, and subsidized marketplace coverage. The bill text notes one in four U.S. children has at least one immigrant parent, and it emphasizes pregnant and postpartum immigrant women, LGBTQ immigrants, and immigrants with disabilities who disproportionately lack coverage [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Lawfully present immigrants and their children

how_it_helps.text: States would be required to cover lawfully residing individuals, including DACA applicants and people with federally authorized presence, under Medicaid and CHIP if they meet normal eligibility rules, replacing the 1996-law five-year waiting bar [S3].

All individuals with federally authorized presence would be treated as lawfully present for exchange eligibility, reduced cost-sharing, premium subsidies, premium tax credits, and Medicaid and CHIP eligibility [S3].

The bill would strike the ACA's limits that restrict marketplace access to citizens and lawful residents, allowing noncitizens ineligible for Medicaid due to immigration status to receive premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions instead [S3].

It would eliminate states' authority to restrict Medicaid eligibility for lawful permanent residents and ensure no sponsor debt accrues under an affidavit of support when a covered immigrant receives Medicaid [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal and state governments would bear the cost of extending Medicaid, CHIP, and marketplace subsidies to hundreds of thousands of lawfully present immigrants who currently have them delayed or withheld. Health insurers would gain new subsidized customers, since the marketplace subsidies would flow through private plans.

drawbacks.text: Extending Medicaid, CHIP, and premium subsidies to newly eligible noncitizens would increase federal and state health spending, the cost Congress's fiscal scorekeepers would have had to estimate; the bill text sets an effective date 90 days after enactment with transition time for states needing to change their plans [S3].

The bill would remove the five-year waiting period for legal permanent residents that the 1996 welfare law imposed, and would shield sponsors from reimbursement liability for a covered immigrant's Medicaid costs, both of which critics of expanded coverage for noncitizens oppose as a matter of cost and policy [S3].
The bill would open ACA marketplace subsidies to undocumented immigrants as well, which is a wider expansion than covering lawfully present people and was certain to draw opposition [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage expansion addresses a concrete, documented gap: lawfully present immigrants are barred or delayed from programs they would otherwise qualify for on income, with serious consequences in maternal health and children's care. The cost is additional federal and state health spending plus a politically contested extension of subsidies to undocumented immigrants, and the bill contains no offsetting savings. It is a real benefit paid for with new public money.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Booker introduced the bill on May 17, 2021 with eight original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1].
Twelve senators ultimately cosponsored: 11 of the 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of the 2 independents; no Republican cosponsored [S4].
The complete action history shows no further action after the referral: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action [S5].
The bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the immigration-status restrictions on Medicaid, CHIP, and marketplace coverage remained in place [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal and state budgets were spared new spending, but the direct beneficiaries of inaction were the status quo: insurers kept out of the newly insured immigrant market, and lawfully present immigrants and DACA recipients remained excluded from Medicaid, CHIP, and subsidized coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supporters lost; immigrants kept current restrictions

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited eight original cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, one of 11 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Ron Wyden, D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it died at referral.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 50 Republicans cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; not one of the 50 Senate Republicans signed on, and the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.note: The bill would have routed new Medicaid, CHIP, and subsidized marketplace enrollment through insurers and private ACA plans, adding paying customers; by dying, it left insurers without that new market. Its interest ran alongside immigrants seeking coverage.

Extending Medicaid, CHIP, and premium subsidies to lawfully present immigrants would have increased public health spending; the bill's defeat avoided that cost while leaving immigrants' coverage gaps in place.
